lanes.lane: constraints — the DO-NOT-REPROPOSE list, plus the open questions the same documents leave standing

findings.claim: The committed-text lag of +9 to +11 s decomposes into chunk-close latency (6-20 s by construction, a policy not an inefficiency), ~5 s to decode a committed chunk at ~0.31 real time, the post-stop polish, and 5-14 ms of everything else — so 85-90% of the lag is decode time plus the deliberate chunking policy.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:13-30 (table at :16-21), :40-41

findings.claim: REFUTED: 'skip the open-tail preview decode' — its return value looks discarded but is the LocalAgreement-2 seed, so killing it adds a full cycle of lag; and REFUTED: 'decode_ratio is blind so the loop is behind' — measured 0.64-0.76x, already inside the <=1.4x target, with stream.decode_ratio at 1.17x and 1.36x across two runs.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:47-48, :28-30

findings.claim: REFUTED: 'shorten the fixed 2.0 s cycle nap' — it is idle slack, not a queue, and polling faster *raises* decode_ratio; and REFUTED: 'cap the VAD re-scan window' — the open region is already bounded by force_cut_sec and a 22 s cap never binds (max observed tail 11.6 s).
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:49-50

findings.claim: REFUTED on correctness, not speed: 'drop word timestamps to skip the DTW alignment' — it silently deletes committed words via the 8-second hallucination gate at transcriber.py:352, and word confidence is now also load-bearing for polish targeting and the uncertain-word underline.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:51; CLAUDE.md:220-223, :249-256

findings.claim: REFUTED: 'drop vad_filter from the post-stop polish pass' — chunks *begin* with the pause they were cut at, so the second pass's VAD does real work rather than duplicating the segmenter's.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:52

findings.claim: REFUTED as below the noise floor: 'cache _project_root()' (0.566 ms against a 1-3 s cycle) and 'prefilter the 151-rule terminology table' (its ASCII safety valve is switched off upstream by the degree sign in measurements.py:47, making the prefilter net *slower* on real MSK reports).
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:53-54

findings.claim: The honest ceiling on preview-side work: deleting the open-tail preview decode entirely — stronger than any of the seven proposals — moved lag only from +10.5 s to +9.1 s, i.e. 1.4 s or about 13%, paid for by deleting the live preview.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:32-41

findings.claim: REFUTED as a target: the 10-stage post-processing pipeline costs 5-14 ms against the ~6,200 ms to decode the same 20 s of audio (0.08% of a cycle, no hidden hotspot), and model loading, the compute_type fallback chain and CPU thread count were each investigated and found 'not the problem'.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:23-26; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:77-78

findings.claim: REFUTED TWICE: shortening the chunks — first because small.en costs a fixed ~4 s per transcribe() call whatever it is handed so halving chunk length nearly doubles total decode, then re-measured on the fast live model (18 tts clips, tiny.en live + small.en polish) where 3/6/8 against the shipped 6/15/20 raised decode 66% (216 s to 358 s), pushed RTF from 0.55 to 0.92 (no headroom under the sub-1.0 constraint), and moved WER 6.66%->7.31% and medical-term error 7.11%->7.56% the wrong way.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:93-97 and :157-175 (table at :163-166)

findings.claim: REFUTED: adding faster-whisper's `hotwords` argument to get more radiology vocabulary into the decoder — get_prompt() spends hotwords and initial_prompt from the *same* 223-token budget so they compete rather than add; measured against the installed tokenizer, radiology_prompt.txt was 1,150 tokens and 927 were discarded.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:99-122 (esp. :103-104, :120-122)

findings.claim: REFUTED as a default swap: Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 is 5.2x faster than Whisper small.en (RTF 0.108 vs 0.565; 70 s vs 358 s on 10.8 min of audio) but doubles the medical-term error rate (3.44% -> 7.12%), the one metric allowed to veto a speed win — verdict 'do not switch', engine kept available behind --engine parakeet.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-accuracy.md:116-147 (table at :121-127, verdict at :129-133)

findings.claim: REFUTED on measurement: the per-word confidence veto on corrections (src/dictation/postprocess/confidence_gate.py, 24 tests) is shipped DISABLED — at ceiling >=0.90 it fired twice in 30 reports and both times blocked a correction that was right, moving every metric the wrong way; separately, raising polish_confidence_ceiling (currently 0.75) to catch confidently-wrong words re-decodes more chunks, spends the Stop headroom, and has deliberately not been changed.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-accuracy.md:59-83 (table at :66-70); docs/dictation-speed-review.md:192-200; src/core/settings.py:61

findings.claim: REJECTED ON COST, not deferred: acoustic rescoring of candidate words for a low-confidence span needs either a forced-alignment API faster-whisper does not expose or one re-decode per candidate, and with a fixed ~3.6 s per transcribe() call N candidate decodes per span breaks the real-time budget outright — revisit only behind an engine that exposes frame posteriors.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-accuracy.md:90-97

findings.claim: Four more already-settled details not to re-litigate: pricing the preview by tail length (open_tail_sec * decode_cost) switched previews off part-way through every chunk and was replaced by pricing per call; requiring LocalAgreement-2 agreement before showing anything put first words at 13.8 s and was replaced by show-the-first-decode-provisionally (13.8 s -> 2.1 s, of which lazy Silero VAD loading was 11 s and preview_min_tail_sec=1.0 s the third part); live beam_size=1 caused repetition so beam=2 is deliberate; and any bench harness feeding arrays must use faster_whisper.audio.decode_audio(path, sampling_rate=16000), because naive nearest-sample resampling of the 22050 Hz clips aliases WER from ~10% to ~62% and reads exactly like a corrupt gold set.
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md:207-219, :197-206, :233-240; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:96-97; docs/dictation-speed-review.md:202-210

levers.lever: Record the `own` gold set: `python -m scripts.eval.build_sets --set own --record`, about 15 minutes of the user's own voice.
levers.mechanism: It does not itself reduce lag; it unblocks every other lever. The tts set is synthetic, generic-radiology vocabulary under unrealistically clean audio, so it scores real-acoustics and MSK-vocabulary changes as noise and can only see the cost of a specialty trade, never its benefit. Confirmed still unrecorded: data/eval/own/ holds manifest.jsonl and five .script.txt files and zero .wav files. Ranked #1 by expected value at docs/dictation-accuracy.md:164-166.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 directly; it is the gate on the 5x-faster-engine lever below, which is worth roughly 4 s of the ~5 s committed-chunk decode
levers.risk: None to the app. The risk is skipping it: any speed change judged only on tts can mangle anatomy invisibly, which is exactly the failure this project exists to prevent.

levers.lever: Wire lexicon biasing into Parakeet's CTC path and re-run the bake-off.
levers.mechanism: Parakeet's doubled term error (7.12% vs 3.44%) was measured with NO radiology vocabulary reaching it at all — the engine reports `hotwords: False` — while Whisper gets the 210-token prompt inside its decoder. Some of that gap is a missing feature, not a worse model, and Parakeet's false-correction rate is already less than half Whisper's (5.56% vs 14.29%, 34 true fixes against 2 bad). Named as the #2 next step at docs/dictation-accuracy.md:167-169 and :137-141.
levers.est_seconds_saved: up to ~4 s per committed chunk if term error closes to Whisper's (RTF 0.108 vs 0.565); 0 if it does not close
levers.risk: Term error is the veto metric. If biasing does not close the 3.44%->7.12% gap the answer is still 'do not switch' — and it must be judged on the `own` set, not tts, or the verdict is uninterpretable.

levers.lever: Use the fast engine for the POST-STOP polish rather than as the live engine.
levers.mechanism: docs/dictation-accuracy.md:155-158 says explicitly that a faster engine is 'worth having for the post-Stop polish, not a cure for a lag that has already been fixed'. The polish currently re-decodes every low-confidence committed chunk plus the open tail at final_beam_size on small.en (src/dictation/worker.py:460-495); measured, that background pass lands at +16.1 s (web) and +17.2 s (desktop) after Stop (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:186-188).
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 s of live lag; roughly 12-15 s off the background polish window, which is what buys headroom to raise polish_confidence_ceiling
levers.risk: The polish is the accuracy backstop for the fast live model. A polish engine with worse term error makes the final report worse than the live text it replaced — the one place a speed win is unambiguously not allowed.

levers.lever: Settle the condition_on_previous_text disagreement by teaching the eval harness to drive the polish path.
levers.mechanism: The two paths disagree in shipped code: live sets it False (src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:445, src/dictation/worker.py:327 and :413, src/ui/web_app.py:869) while the confidence-targeted polish sets it True (src/dictation/worker.py:466 and :492). With it True each decoded segment pushes the 223-token prompt further out of the window, trading vocabulary priming for continuity. The harness decodes one-shot and never exercises the polish path, so there is no way to measure which is better; docs/dictation-accuracy.md:110-114 marks it 'Open, not fixed' and :170-171 ranks it #3.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0-1 s per polished chunk (a shorter prompt decodes marginally faster); the real payoff is accuracy, not seconds
levers.risk: Setting it False in the polish could break sentence continuity across chunk boundaries; setting it True everywhere evicts the radiology prompt from the live path. Both directions stay unmeasurable until the harness can run the polish path.

levers.lever: Re-choose which 223 tokens reach the decoder, now that the ordering mechanism exists.
levers.mechanism: Whisper's prompt slot is 223 tokens and radiology_prompt.txt was 1,150, so 927 were discarded — and because Whisper keeps the LAST 223, what survived was generic MRI/ultrasound physics vocabulary while ACL, PCL, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis and glenohumeral were dropped (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:99-118). The shipped prompt is now 210 tokens spent on musculoskeletal and trauma terms, and full-30-clip medical-term error was flat (3.40% -> 3.29%) because tts cannot reward that trade by construction (docs/dictation-accuracy.md:50-57). Explicitly left unfinished pending the `own` set.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 s; this is a pure accuracy lever whose value is that it can PAY FOR a speed lever elsewhere by absorbing that lever's term-error cost
levers.risk: A third claimant on the same budget is the user's learned terms (capped at 80, about 216 tokens, enough to evict the shipped vocabulary entirely); the current fix is ordering — learned terms are written first so they are the ones dropped (docs/dictation-accuracy.md:104-108). Any re-ordering must preserve that.

levers.lever: Give the confidence veto (confidence_gate.py, built, 24 tests, shipped off) its fair hearing on the `own` set.
levers.mechanism: It was measured only on synthetic audio 'where nearly every word scores high, the signal barely varies at all' — so the instrument, not the mechanism, may be what failed. A real microphone and a real accent produce confidences that actually vary. One setting turns it on (docs/dictation-accuracy.md:80-83).
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 s; it is a false-correction lever, and a lower false-correction rate is what would let a faster, noisier engine be accepted
levers.risk: On the evidence so far it subtracts: it blocked two right corrections in 30 reports and moved every metric the wrong way. Re-enabling it without the own set is simply repeating a refuted experiment.

levers.lever: Measure a chunk policy BETWEEN the two points that have data — only 6/15/20 and 3/6/8 have ever been run.
levers.mechanism: Chunk-close latency is the single largest lag term (6-20 s by construction, docs/dictation-speed-review.md:18) and it is policy, not inefficiency; M6 already made the knobs tunable and they sit in src/core/settings.py:39-41. Halving to 3/6/8 was refuted on RTF 0.92 and worse accuracy, but nothing between the two has been measured — for example lowering chunk_soft_max_sec alone while leaving chunk_min_sec at 6.0, which changes when a pause is *accepted* rather than how short a chunk may be.
levers.est_seconds_saved: plausibly 2-4 s of chunk-close latency if a mid-point holds RTF near 0.6-0.7; unmeasured
levers.risk: The refuted 3/6/8 run is the warning: more chunks means more fixed ~1 s decode calls, and RTF above about 0.9 leaves no headroom on this CPU-only machine. Must be run through scripts.eval.run_eval with RTF and medical-term error read side by side, never judged by feel.

levers.lever: Decouple what the user sees as SETTLED from when a chunk CLOSES.
levers.mechanism: Inferred, not named in the docs, so treat it as unvalidated. The complaint is about committed text, and chunk-close latency is 6-20 s of that by construction — yet the preview already shows those words, pinned and never taken back after the single permitted first correction (CLAUDE.md:197-206). If pinned preview text were promoted to committed status at a pause boundary rather than waiting for the chunk to close, the perceived commit lag falls with no change to decode cost at all.
levers.est_seconds_saved: up to the chunk-close term itself, 6-20 s of perceived lag, at zero decode cost — speculative until measured
levers.risk: Directly touches the hard constraint that confirmed text must not un-write itself: promoting preview text to committed means the later closed-chunk decode may disagree with text already presented as permanent. The ledger's decode-once guarantee (src/dictation/stream/ledger.py) needs re-examining before anyone writes code.

uncertainties: The +9 to +11 s committed-text figure is from 2026-07-28, before the tiny.en live-model split (2026-09-01) and before the preview repricing. No post-split measurement of COMMITTED-text lag exists in these documents; every 2026-09-01 number measures either first-words-on-screen (4.7 s, 4.9 s, 6.9 s) or the background polish (+16.1 s, +17.2 s). The user's current complaint may be against a lag budget nobody has re-decomposed.

Every accuracy number in both documents comes from the synthetic tts set. docs/dictation-accuracy.md:6-11 states outright these are vocabulary numbers that 'say nothing about what a real microphone and a real accent do'. Any refutation resting on a term-error delta — Parakeet, chunk shortening, the confidence veto — is refuted on an instrument that cannot see this app's actual acoustics.

dictation_settings.json sets model_size to small.en while src/core/settings.py:14 defaults it to base.en, and the file still carries the superseded live_window_sec (25.0) and commit_lag_sec (5.0) keys that docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:131-136 says no longer exist. Check which values a given run actually used before quoting any RTF at the user.

The 2026-09-01 chunk re-measurement used 18 tts clips and the document itself notes an 8-clip run had the two accuracy rows the other way round, so the accuracy half of that refutation sits inside the noise. Only the decode/RTF half (216 s -> 358 s, 0.55 -> 0.92) is solid.

The 'seven proposals' table at docs/dictation-speed-review.md:45-54 actually contains eight rows; one row is a refuted claim ('decode_ratio is blind') rather than a proposal. All eight are listed above.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md sections 2, 3 and its tunable-knobs table are explicitly marked superseded by the chunk-once rebuild (:12-18, :131-136). It is cited above only for facts it flags as still current: live beam=1 causing repetition, and model loading / compute_type / thread count not being the problem.

lanes.lane: Desktop front-end: does it share or duplicate the live rules?

findings.claim: The genuinely shared core is small: segmenter.py (ChunkPolicy/cut_chunks), ledger.py (ChunkLedger/close_sentence), tail.py (LocalAgreement2), vad.py, and five helpers in rules.py (build_context_prompt, mean_confidence, low_confidence_words, rms, AdaptiveFloor, should_skip_preview). Everything else about the live loop is written twice.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/worker.py:63-73 imports vs src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:29-39 imports; rules.py:1-9 docstring states the intent

findings.claim: Only the preview-skip PREDICATE is shared; the state machine around it is copy-pasted, including the same magic constants (0.9 decay while skipping, 0.6/0.4 cost smoothing, _preview_earliest = now + cost).
findings.evidence: worker.py:346-362 and worker.py:426-427 vs live_session.py:210-226 and live_session.py:312-313; rules.should_skip_preview is rules.py:122-157 and holds no state

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE: the minimum-tail gate before a preview decode (preview_min_tail_sec) exists only on the web. The desktop will spend a full ~0.7-1.5s tiny.en decode on a fraction of a second of audio, which is exactly the waste the web removed to get first words from 13.8s to 2.1s.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:299 `if len(clip) < self.preview_min_tail_sec * self.sr: return self._agreement.stable()`; no occurrence of preview_min_tail_sec in worker.py or recording_session.py (grep over src/dictation and src/ui); the setting exists at src/core/settings.py:59 and is read only at src/ui/web_app.py:929-931

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE: low-confidence word marking is web-only end to end. The desktop never reads uncertain_word_confidence, never calls low_confidence_words, and no desktop view renders a mark, so a desktop report gives no signal about words the decoder guessed at.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:104,175-178 and web_app.py:951-953 and src/ui/frontends/app.js:1394-1412; grep for 'uncertain' returns zero hits in src/ui/main_window.py, src/ui/views.py, src/ui/term_marks.py and zero in worker.py

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE: the web closes the still-open tail with the fast model before handing the report back; the desktop hands back committed text plus the LocalAgreement-2 preview instead. If previews were being skipped when Stop was pressed, the desktop hand-back carries a stale _last_stable and can be missing most of the last chunk, which is the exact '20 of 48 words handed back' failure the web fixed.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:325-355 (close_open_tail_fast) called at web_app.py:1072; desktop hand-back is recording_session.py:308-333 reading window._last_raw_transcript, which is set at recording_session.py:347 from worker.py:364-373 (committed_text + stable_tail, where stable_tail is worker.py:356 self._last_stable when skipping)

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE: the web puts a full stop on the finished report; the desktop does not. ledger.close_sentence is applied only at paragraph gaps inside committed_text, so the desktop's last sentence ends bare.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:405 `final = close_sentence(self._post.process(raw, 0)[0])`; worker.py:508 `full_text = self._ledger.committed_text` with no close_sentence; ledger.py:109 is the only other call site

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE in the provisional/committed contract: the desktop concatenates preview into the committed string, so the 10-stage pipeline runs over provisional words and the editor renders them identically to frozen text. The web deliberately post-processes only the committed half and ships preview as its own field so the page can dim it.
findings.evidence: worker.py:364-373 merges then emits one string; recording_session.py:347-356 submits that whole string to the pipeline; live_session.py:228-234 with the comment at 229-231, and LiveUpdate's docstring live_session.py:50-58 stating the rule the desktop breaks

findings.claim: Desktop-only per-cycle cost: a soundfile header stat plus a seek-and-read off the growing WAV every cycle. The web slices an in-memory buffer.
findings.evidence: worker.py:239 self._audio_length() -> sf.info (worker.py:536-549), worker.py:298 self._read_audio(tail_start) (worker.py:551-587, wrapped in perf.stage 'worker.read_audio'); live_session.py:196-198 is `buf, total = self._buf, self._len` then a slice

findings.claim: Desktop-only idle time: after every cycle the worker sleeps for half the cycle's WALL time, capped at 2.0s. A cycle that commits one chunk (~1.5s) and runs a preview (~1.4s) therefore parks the loop for ~1.5s before it can even look for the next chunk cut. The web starts the next cycle as soon as live_cycle_sec (0.5s) has passed and the previous task is done.
findings.evidence: worker.py:271-277 `sleep_time = max(0.4, min(decode_sec * 0.5, 2.0))` where decode_sec is the full cycle duration returned by worker.py:375; web_app.py:1044-1046 `if time.time() - last_cycle >= cycle_sec and (cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done())`

findings.claim: That desktop-only pacing is consistent with the only head-to-head measurement on file: same 30s clip, first text on screen 4.9s on the web versus 6.9s on the desktop, and the accuracy pass landing 1.1s later on the desktop.
findings.evidence: docs/dictation-speed-review.md:180-190 (the table under 'Update 2026-09-01: Stop no longer waits, on either front-end')

findings.claim: Stop is slower to take effect on the desktop: finalize() only sets a flag, and the loop notices it at the top of the next iteration, so up to 2.0s of the sleep above elapses before the polish begins. The web explicitly awaits the in-flight cycle and then proceeds immediately.
findings.evidence: worker.py:201-203 finalize(), consumed at worker.py:238 and worker.py:261-268; called from recording_session.py:303-305; web equivalent at web_app.py:1057-1061

findings.claim: SAFETY DIVERGENCE: the web refuses to commit a chunk whose end runs past the audio it actually sliced this cycle; the desktop has no such check, and its total_samples (from the WAV header) comes from a different call than its audio (a separate read), so the two can legitimately disagree on a file still being written. numpy would clamp silently and ledger.commit would advance the open frontier past audio that was never decoded.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:252-259 (the explicit guard and its comment) versus worker.py:309-310 `local = slice(...); chunk_audio = tail_audio[local]` with no bounds test; the two sources are worker.py:239 (sf.info) and worker.py:298 (read); the frontier advance is ledger.py:148-151

findings.claim: DIVERGENCE in decode parameters: every web decode pins temperature=0.0, while the desktop's post-Stop polish passes no temperature at all, which transcriber.py turns into Whisper's fallback ladder [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8] - up to five re-decodes of a segment. Cuts both ways: it costs the desktop background time, and it means the two front-ends' polish passes are not the same decode.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:448 temperature=0.0 for all stages; worker.py:459-470 and worker.py:488-495 omit temperature; default is types.py:86 (None) and transcriber.py:276 expands None to the ladder

findings.claim: COMMIT-POLICY COUPLING: a change in the streaming core would need four desktop edits, and two places would silently keep the old behaviour. Needs editing: worker.py:293-375 (_run_cycle's own commit loop, a private copy of live_session._commit_closed), worker.py:434-517 (the desktop's own polish, a private copy of finalize), worker.py:373 (the committed_len it hands the incremental post-processor), recording_session.py:261-276 (the constructor arg list). Silently unchanged: any new gate added to LiveSession only (as preview_min_tail_sec and close_open_tail_fast already are), and the desktop's hand-back, which reads a UI-side cached string rather than asking the ledger.
findings.evidence: worker.py:293-375, worker.py:434-517, worker.py:373, recording_session.py:261-276, recording_session.py:319; contrast live_session.py:245-277 and live_session.py:357-410

levers.lever: Wire preview_min_tail_sec into LiveTranscribeWorker and apply it in _decode_open_tail, mirroring live_session.py:299 (return self._agreement.stable(), do not clear).
levers.mechanism: Stops the desktop burning a whole ~0.7-1.5s tiny.en decode on sub-second tails. On the web this was one of the three changes credited with 13.8s -> 2.1s; the decode it saves is a decode the committed chunks get instead.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 1-2s off first words, and one preview slot per chunk returned to committed decoding
levers.risk: None to anatomy accuracy: the preview is never committed. Only risk is the preview appearing slightly later at the very start of each chunk.

levers.lever: Replace worker.py:276-277's sleep with the web's cadence: wake on a fixed live_cycle_sec (settings.py:87, default 0.5) rather than sleeping for half the last cycle's wall time.
levers.mechanism: The current formula makes the loop idle longest exactly after the most expensive cycles, which are the cycles that just committed a chunk and therefore have the next chunk waiting. That idle time is pure added lag on the committed text, which is the user's actual complaint.
levers.est_seconds_saved: up to 1.5-2.0s per commit cycle on the desktop; plausibly most of the measured 2.0s desktop/web first-text gap
levers.risk: A tighter loop raises the desktop's CPU share, which could crowd the decoder. Mitigate by keeping the existing guard that a cycle never overlaps itself, exactly as web_app.py:1044-1046 does.

levers.lever: Give the desktop stop path a close_open_tail_fast equivalent (or better: call the shared one) before _hand_back_live_text, and hand back ledger text rather than window._last_raw_transcript.
levers.mechanism: Today the desktop's hand-back can be committed text plus a stale preview. One fast decode (~1.5s here) buys a complete report; the current path can hand back a report missing the last chunk with nothing saying so.
levers.est_seconds_saved: costs ~1.5s at Stop, removes an unbounded gap where the last chunk arrives only with the polish
levers.risk: Adds ~1.5s to the currently +0.0s hand-back. The tail would be fast-model text, so it must be force-polished like live_session._forced_polish_index (live_session.py:371-372) or an anatomical word decoded by tiny.en could survive into the report.

levers.lever: Add the chunk-past-tail guard from live_session.py:252-259 to worker.py:309.
levers.mechanism: Prevents committing a decode of the wrong seconds and advancing the ledger frontier past audio that was never decoded. On the desktop the header length and the audio read are two separate calls against a file still being written, so the mismatch this guards is reachable.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0s; it is a correctness fix, not a speed one
levers.risk: Defers a chunk by one cycle in the rare case it fires. No accuracy downside.

levers.lever: Move the preview-skip state (cost smoothing, decay, _preview_earliest, _last_stable) out of both loops into a small class in stream/rules.py that both instantiate.
levers.mechanism: The four constants are currently duplicated at worker.py:346-362/426-427 and live_session.py:210-226/312-313. Any future tuning of the preview budget otherwise lands in one front-end only, which is the documented recurring defect in this repo.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0s directly; it is what stops the next speed fix from being web-only
levers.risk: Pure refactor; the existing test_stream_rules.py covers the predicate but not the state machine, so add a test for the decay and the earliest-start gate.

levers.lever: Pin temperature=0.0 in worker.py's two polish decodes (worker.py:459-470, 488-495), or pin the fallback ladder on both front-ends.
levers.mechanism: Right now the two front-ends run different decoders in the polish pass, so a desktop measurement cannot be compared with a web one. transcriber.py:276 expands None into a five-temperature fallback.
levers.est_seconds_saved: variable background seconds after Stop; 0s of live lag
levers.risk: Removing the fallback can make Whisper keep a degenerate/repetitive segment it would otherwise have retried, which is an accuracy risk in the direction this app cares about. Measure on the eval harness before choosing which way to converge.

levers.lever: Retire worker.py's loop: run stream.LiveSession on the desktop's QThread, feeding it blocks from audio.py instead of polling the WAV, and keep worker.py only as the Qt signal shell.

After each preview decode the next one is blocked for as long as the last one took, so during preview-only stretches the browser gets a genuinely new message roughly every 2 decodes, i.e. about 2.6-3.0 s on this machine.

findings.claim: On a cycle that closes a chunk, the newly committed text is NOT sent until that same cycle has also finished its preview decode: one cycle produces exactly one message, built after both decodes.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:205 (_commit_closed) -> 210-226 (preview decode) -> 234 (LiveUpdate built) -> 242 returned; src/ui/web_app.py:997 awaits `session.cycle` then sends at 1019. The dedupe's exact behaviour on the first skip cycle after a live cycle (state changes live -> catching_up, so one extra message IS sent with unchanged text) is read from code; I did not observe the resulting message sequence on the wire.

Whether the browser coalesces several WebSocket messages arriving close together into one task-queue turn is not something I checked; if it does, two messages from lever 1 could paint in the same frame and the split would show no benefit.
