levers.lever: Promote the LocalAgreement-2 confirmed prefix from display-only to committed text: when two consecutive open-tail decodes agree on a word, write it into the ledger instead of only painting it dimmed. This is what Whisper-Streaming (Machacek, Dabre, Bojar, ACL 2023 demo) actually does; this repo implements the algorithm but throws its output away.
levers.mechanism: Removes the two dominant terms at once. A word's commit latency stops being (wait for a >=6s chunk to close) + (queue behind a preview) + (decode) and becomes (two preview cycles) ~= 2 x 1.5s. It also removes work rather than adding it: the preview decode at live_session.py:279-314 currently produces text that is discarded and then re-earned by a second decode of the same samples at :267.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 4-6 s of the 9-11 s
levers.risk: The largest risk in this whole list. It breaks the guarantee the ledger exists to state (ledger.py:1-13) and moves the commit decision off a VAD-verified silence boundary onto an arbitrary mid-word audio edge. Whisper's failure mode at a truncated edge is not a dropped word but a fluent invention, which is exactly the class the 8-second hallucination gate exists to catch. And the committed text is then tiny.en's, at 9.4% medical-term error against small.en's 3.4% (speed-review.md:78-82). Unsafe on its own; only defensible paired with lever 2.

levers.lever: Run the accurate model as a continuous background corrector a chunk or two behind the live frontier, instead of only after Stop. Walk _ledger.low_confidence_indices() on its own task while recording, calling the existing ChunkLedger.replace().
levers.mechanism: The two-model design is already half of the standard two-pass architecture (small streaming pass + large rescoring pass, e.g. Sainath et al. 2019 two-pass RNN-T + LAS). Here the second pass is scheduled only at Stop (live_session.py:379-394, called from web_app.py:1089). Moving it to run during dictation does not make the first word appear sooner, but it converts fast text into accurate text seconds after it lands rather than minutes, which is what makes lever 1 or 6 acceptable at all.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 s of first-appearance lag; converts committed text from tiny.en quality to small.en quality within ~5-10 s of commit instead of at Stop
levers.risk: CPU contention: transcriber.py:166 gives both models 14 threads on 16 cores. A small.en call measured ~4 s alone (speed-review.md:138-145) would stretch and be stretched by the live tiny.en calls, so the live loop could fall behind while chasing accuracy. Needs lever 3 first. Also inherits the confident-and-wrong blind spot in speed-review.md:192-200: the corrector only revisits chunks whose confidence was low.

levers.lever: Give each engine its own intra-op thread budget instead of both taking cpu_count-2. E.g. live engine 10 threads, corrector 4, at transcriber.py:166.
levers.mechanism: Makes lever 2 mechanically possible. Right now two concurrent decodes request 28 threads on 16 cores, so the OS scheduler decides which of the two clinical paths degrades, rather than the design deciding.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 s directly; it is the precondition for lever 2's benefit
levers.risk: Each individual decode gets slower. If the live engine drops below the threads it needs, first-word latency regresses toward the 13.8 s figure the 2026-09-01 work just fixed. Must be measured per-engine, not assumed.

levers.lever: Give committed-chunk decodes their own task, separate from the preview, so a chunk that reaches a VAD boundary never queues behind an in-flight preview decode. Today both live inside one cycle_task guarded at web_app.py:1043-1045.
levers.mechanism: Attacks the queue term directly: a preview costs 0.7-2.2 s measured, and a chunk that becomes committable one tenth of a second into one waits out the whole call before its own decode even starts.
levers.risk: Two decodes at once, which is the same oversubscription problem as lever 2, on a smaller scale (both would be tiny.en). Also, live_session.cycle() is explicitly documented as not written to survive two concurrent entries (live_session.py:185-195), so the split must be done in the session, not by removing the web loop's guard.

levers.lever: Re-measure the shorter chunk policy (3/6/8) with the preview decode switched off, and compare against the shipped 6/15/20 with the preview on.
levers.mechanism: The existing refutation gave RTF 0.92 for 3/6/8, but the preview was running and is designed to eat half the wall clock (live_session.py:122-128). Shorter chunks and a live preview are two ways to buy the same thing, low-latency visible text, and the app is currently paying for both. Spending the entire preview budget on shorter committed chunks may land under RTF 0.7 with real permanent text instead of provisional text.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 2-4 s if it survives; 0 s if it does not
levers.risk: None to run: it is a measurement, not a change. If adopted, the risk is the one the refutation already found: more chunks means more calls at ~0.7 s fixed each, and both accuracy metrics moved the wrong way at 3/6/8 (WER 6.66->7.31%, term error 7.11->7.56%), though the doc itself calls that gap noise.

levers.lever: Commit by distance from the audio edge rather than by agreement count: faster-whisper already returns per-word timestamps, so commit every word in the open-tail decode that ends more than K ms before the end of the decoded clip, and leave the rest provisional.
levers.mechanism: Same latency win as lever 1 (words become permanent from the preview decode, not from a chunk close) but it targets the actual failure mechanism instead of a proxy. Whisper invents text at a truncated edge; a word that ended 1.5 s before the edge had full acoustic right-context and is not an edge artefact. Agreement-count commits, by contrast, can confirm two decodes that made the same edge mistake twice.
levers.risk: K is an unmeasured tuning knob and a too-small K commits exactly the edge hallucinations this is meant to avoid. Word timestamps come from cross-attention DTW and are known-imprecise; the repo already depends on them elsewhere (rules.py:177-199, and speed-review.md:51 records that removing them breaks the hallucination gate), so their accuracy at a chunk edge specifically is untested here.

levers.lever: Run the Parakeet TDT experiment that was left open: wire lexicon biasing into it, then use it as the LIVE engine with Whisper small.en as the background corrector from lever 2.
levers.mechanism: Parakeet is a Transducer, the only architecture family in this repo that is natively frame-synchronous rather than window-padded, so it is the only route to a decode cost that scales with audio rather than sitting at a 0.7 s per-call floor. It is already installed and already behind the swap-seam (asr/factory.py:19, engines/parakeet_engine.py; onnx-asr present on this machine). Measured RTF 0.108 versus small.en's 0.565 buys enough headroom to run short chunks and a continuous corrector at the same time.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 3-6 s, contingent on the biasing experiment
levers.risk: The engine swap alone is already refuted on the veto metric: medical-term error 7.12% versus Whisper small.en 3.44% (dictation-accuracy.md:120-131). The entire case rests on unproven lexicon biasing closing a 2x anatomy gap, and the adapter reports hotwords=False today, so the biasing path does not exist yet. Do not ship this on a speed argument.

uncertainties: The 9-11 s committed-lag figure is from docs/dictation-speed-review.md:12-13, dated 2026-07-28, BEFORE the live_model_size split of 2026-09-01 that took first words from 15.9 s to 4.7 s. I found no post-split measurement of committed-word lag anywhere in the repo. Every seconds figure I attribute below is against a number that may already be stale; measure it before acting on any lever.

My ~4.9 s mean endpoint wait is arithmetic over two published ratios (2.2 chunks per clip, 21.6 s per clip), not an observed chunk-length distribution. Real dictation pause structure could put it anywhere from 3 s to 8 s.

Whether two concurrent ctranslate2 models at 14 threads each actually contend badly on this 16-core box, or the OS schedules it acceptably, is untested. Levers 2, 3 and 4 all hinge on it and none of them is safe to propose as a finished plan until it is measured.

Whether LocalAgreement-2 agreement on tiny.en is precise enough on anatomical vocabulary is completely untested. Two decodes agreeing is agreement about tiny.en's biases, not evidence of correctness, and the whole case for lever 1 rests on it.

Citation confidence: I am confident about LocalAgreement (Liu et al. 2020, partial hypothesis selection) and Whisper-Streaming (Machacek, Dabre, Bojar, ACL 2023 system demo), which is the paper this repo's tail.py is implementing. I recall the others more loosely and would verify before writing any of them into docs: two-pass RNN-T + LAS rescoring (Sainath et al. 2019), WeNet U2/U2++ CTC-prefix-beam plus attention rescoring, MoChA monotonic chunkwise attention, Emformer. The mechanism claims about them stand on architecture, not on my memory of the papers.

No `own` gold set exists (real acoustics, MSK vocabulary) per dictation-accuracy.md:173-177, so every lever here can currently only be scored on synthetic TTS audio, which is exactly the material on which the medical-term-error veto is least trustworthy. Recording it is still the highest-value action in the repo and it blocks honest evaluation of levers 1, 5, 6 and 7.

lanes.lane: chunk-close policy: what makes a word wait before it is committed, and whether the LocalAgreement-2 stable prefix can be committed progressively instead

findings.claim: A cut point can only be the end of a speech mark that has ANOTHER speech mark after it, so a pause only closes a chunk once the speaker starts talking again; a trailing pause closes nothing.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/segmenter.py:94-98 (`if marks[i].end_sample < marks[i+1].start_sample`, loop `range(len(marks)-1)`). Ran cut_chunks(12s audio, one mark 0-6.5s) -> [(0.0, 12.0, closed=False)]: no chunk closes at all despite 5.5s of trailing silence.

findings.claim: The policy deliberately picks the LATEST usable pause up to chunk_soft_max_sec, so plentiful pauses do not shorten chunks; they lengthen them toward 15s.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/segmenter.py:107-111 (`within_soft[-1]`). Ran cut_chunks(30s, a 1.7s speech mark every 2s) -> cuts at 13.7s and 27.7s, not at 6.x s. Defaults chunk_min_sec=6.0 / soft_max=15.0 / force_cut=20.0 at segmenter.py:30-32 and src/core/settings.py:39-41.

findings.claim: With no pause at all the chunk is force-cut at exactly chunk_force_cut_sec, and only once the buffer already runs past it.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/segmenter.py:114-116 (`elif force_pt < total_samples`). Ran cut_chunks(45s, one unbroken 45s mark) -> closed chunks (0,20) and (20,40), open tail (40,45).

findings.claim: The VAD gate adds ~0.5s before a pause is even a candidate: the silence must last 300ms, and the cut is placed 200ms after true speech end because marks are padded.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/vad.py:30-34 and 43-49 (`min_silence_duration_ms=300`, `speech_pad_ms=200`).

findings.claim: After the cut exists, the web loop waits up to live_cycle_sec (0.5s) AND for the previous cycle to finish, because a new cycle only starts when the last task is done.
findings.evidence: src/ui/web_app.py:965 (`cycle_sec` from `live_cycle_sec`, 0.5 in dictation_settings.json) and web_app.py:1044 (`if time.time() - last_cycle >= cycle_sec and (cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done())`); the comment at web_app.py:982-984 says session.cycle() is not written to survive two concurrent runs.

findings.claim: A closing chunk is decoded at the START of a cycle but the open-tail preview runs at the END of the previous one, so a commit queues behind a full preview decode.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:205 (`self._commit_closed(...)`) versus live_session.py:225 (`self._decode_open_tail(...)`), both inside the single-threaded `cycle()`; the whole cycle runs on one worker thread (`anyio.to_thread.run_sync(session.cycle)`, web_app.py:996).

findings.claim: The committed-chunk decode asks for word confidence, which measurably costs +0.6 to +1.6s per call on tiny.en; the preview decode does not ask for it.
findings.evidence: live_session.py:267-270 (`want_confidence=True`) vs live_session.py:305-308 (`want_confidence=False`). Measured on data/bench_audio/chest_long.wav, tiny.en, beam 2, best of 3: 3s clip 1.22s->1.88s, 6s 0.65->1.23, 10s 1.37->2.18, 15s 1.78->3.32, 20s 3.44->4.95, 25s 3.78->5.09.

findings.claim: On tiny.en a decode call is NOT flat with clip length: it rises ~3.5x from a 3s clip to a 25s clip, contradicting the flat-cost premise the preview throttle is built on.
findings.evidence: 5 reps interleaved, same clip, beam 2, no word timestamps (min/median seconds): 3s 0.95/1.17, 6s 1.69/2.00, 10s 1.86/2.49, 15s 2.08/3.44, 20s 2.75/4.75, 25s 3.30/4.29. The flatness claim (1.33s@3s, 1.36s@6s, 1.52s@25s) is asserted at src/dictation/stream/rules.py:143-147 and repeated in CLAUDE.md; those numbers are from the small.en era where the encoder dominates.

findings.claim: Because cost grows with tail length and preview_max_lag_sec is 3.0, the preview switches itself OFF on long open tails and the loop reports catching_up: the same failure the current formula was written to fix, reached by a different route.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/rules.py:155-157 (`return preview_cost_sec > max_lag_sec`), live_session.py:210-226 (skip path, STATE_CATCHING_UP), live_session.py:313 (`self._preview_earliest = time.time() + cost`), preview_max_lag_sec=3.0 in dictation_settings.json; measured 20s-tail cost 2.75s min / 4.75s median crosses that ceiling.

findings.claim: LocalAgreement-2's stable prefix is a bare string with no sample offset, while ChunkLedger.commit demands absolute start/end samples and refuses anything that does not start exactly at the open frontier.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/tail.py:41-48 and 68-105 (everything is `.split()` on text) versus src/dictation/stream/ledger.py:136-151 (raises unless `chunk.closed` and `chunk.start_sample == self._open_start`). The only source of a sample offset is Word.start/end, src/dictation/asr/types.py:19-25, which needs want_word_confidence=True on the preview.

findings.claim: A progressively-committed chunk would carry mean_confidence=None and the post-Stop polish silently skips every None, so the fast model would become the final authority on most of the report.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/ledger.py:153-164 (`if c.mean_confidence is not None and c.mean_confidence < ceiling`), fed by live_session.py:273 (`mean_confidence(result)`); the preview result has no words at all (live_session.py:307 `want_confidence=False`), and src/dictation/stream/rules.py:42-50 returns None when no segment reported a confidence.

findings.claim: The ledger's sentence-close / paragraph break only fires across a chunk that committed EMPTY text, because chunks are always contiguous so the sample gap is otherwise exactly zero.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/ledger.py:100-115 (`gap_sec = (c.start_sample - prev_end)/sr`, with `if not c.text: continue` at 104-105). Ran it: contiguous chunks -> 'the lungs are clear no effusion'; the same two with an empty chunk between -> 'the lungs are clear.\nno effusion'. Progressive commits are contiguous and non-empty, so they never trigger it.

findings.claim: Cutting a chunk mid-speech leaves the next chunk with no way to recover context: chunks never overlap, there is no boundary-dedup step, the prompt deliberately excludes committed text, and live chunks decode with condition_on_previous_text=False at beam 2.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/rules.py:22-26 ('Chunks never overlap in this design, so there is no boundary-dedup step to lean on'); live_session.py:414-450 (`condition: bool = False` default, passed as `condition_on_previous_text`), live_session.py:267-270 (chunk decode passes no `condition`), live_beam_size=2 in dictation_settings.json.

findings.claim: Progressive commit has only one force-polish slot to reuse, so at Stop it either re-decodes ~100 short chunks with small.en or re-decodes none of them.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:139 (`self._forced_polish_index: Optional[int] = None`), set at 355, consumed at 371 (`if self._forced_polish_index is not None and ... not in targets`). docs/dictation-speed-review.md records the property this would destroy: report handed back +0.0s, accuracy pass lands +16.1s (web).

levers.lever: Cap the PREVIEW clip to the last N seconds of the open tail (new knob, e.g. preview_max_tail_sec = 8) instead of decoding the whole open tail in _decode_open_tail.
levers.mechanism: Measured, preview cost tracks clip length on tiny.en (2.75-4.75s at 20s of tail vs 1.69-2.00s at 6s). live_session.py:313 blocks the next preview for exactly the last one's cost and rules.py:155-157 drops previews entirely once cost > preview_max_lag_sec=3.0, so a long tail throttles and then silences the preview. A shorter preview clip roughly halves the cost and doubles the LocalAgreement-2 cadence.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 1-3s off perceived (preview) lag; 0s off committed lag
levers.risk: Display-only path (live_session.py:279-314), so kept text and medical-term accuracy are untouched. Real risks: LocalAgreement2._previous would compare two different audio windows unless the window is anchored, and the preview would show only recent words, so the committed+preview join in the front-end needs checking. Must not be applied to _commit_closed.

levers.lever: Add the last speech mark's end as a cut candidate when the audio after it is already silent for >= min_silence, i.e. stop requiring a FOLLOWING speech mark in segmenter.cut_chunks.
levers.mechanism: Verified: a 6.5s utterance followed by 5.5s of silence closes nothing today (segmenter.py:94-98). The commonest real behaviour, say a sentence then pause to think, currently waits for the radiologist to speak again before the words they already said can be committed.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0s in continuous speech; seconds to tens of seconds in the pause-heavy case, capped today only by the 20s force cut
levers.risk: Lowest of any lever here: the cut is still at a VAD-confirmed silence boundary and the chunk is still >= chunk_min_sec, so nothing is cut mid-word and the accuracy premise at segmenter.py:4-10 is preserved. Small chance of freezing a trailing word Whisper would have finished differently with more audio. Needs the same change in the desktop copy (worker.py:297-339).

levers.lever: Lower chunk_soft_max_sec from 15.0 to ~9-10, leaving chunk_min_sec at 6.0 and chunk_force_cut_sec at 20.0.
levers.mechanism: segmenter.py:110-111 takes the LATEST pause up to soft_max, so the policy actively pushes chunks toward 15s (verified: pauses every 2s still produced a 13.7s chunk). Mean wait for a mid-chunk word is about half the chunk length, so 6/10/20 caps it near 4s instead of 7s, while every cut stays at a VAD silence boundary.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 2.5-3s off committed lag
levers.risk: NOT the change docs/dictation-speed-review.md:163-168 refuted: that was 3/6/8, which also halved min_sec and doubled chunk count (medical-term error 7.11%->7.56%, RTF 0.55->0.92). This keeps the 6s floor. But chunk count still rises ~40%, and on the measured curve a 10s chunk costs 1.86s vs 2.08s for 15s, so decode per second of audio rises ~0.14 -> ~0.19 and RTF moves toward ~0.7. Must be re-measured on scripts/eval before shipping.

levers.lever: Split the web cycle into a commit task that never waits and a preview task that may be dropped, so a closed chunk is not queued behind the previous cycle's preview decode.
levers.mechanism: web_app.py:1044 gates a new cycle on `cycle_task.done()`, and live_session.cycle() runs _commit_closed (line 205) only after the previous cycle's _decode_open_tail (line 225) has returned. Measured preview cost on a long tail is 2.75-4.75s, all of which sits between a chunk closing and its text appearing.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0-4.8s, sharply worse on long tails
levers.risk: Real refactor, not a flag: web_app.py:982-984 states cycle() is not written to survive two concurrent runs. The ledger and LocalAgreement2 mutations must stay on one thread; getting this wrong reintroduces the duplicated-seconds bug the snapshot comment at live_session.py:185-195 describes.

levers.lever: Progressive commit of the LocalAgreement-2 stable prefix, in the only de-risked form: promote the stable prefix ONLY up to the last Silero speech-mark end inside the open tail, ignoring chunk_min_sec and the following-mark requirement.
levers.mechanism: Keeps the silence-boundary invariant (segmenter.py:4-10) while removing the two waits that are pure policy: the 6s floor and the need for the speaker to resume. Needs want_word_confidence=True on the preview to map words to samples (types.py:19-25), which measured at +0.59s (6s clip) to +1.55s (15s clip), and that same flag simultaneously supplies the mean_confidence the polish gate needs (ledger.py:153-164).
levers.est_seconds_saved: 3-6s off committed lag
levers.risk: Chunks shorter than 6s are the direction docs/dictation-speed-review.md:163-168 measured as worse for medical-term error, so this needs the eval harness, not judgement. _forced_polish_index (live_session.py:139) must become a set or Stop cost explodes. Sub-6s chunks newly expose single-word real dictation to the whole-segment hallucination gate (transcriber.py:369-372, applied at :300), which deletes a segment whose entire text is e.g. 'you'.

levers.lever: Naive progressive commit of the stable prefix at an arbitrary word boundary, cutting mid-speech. Listed to rule it out, not to try.
levers.mechanism: Would remove the whole 0-20s chunk-close wait in one step.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 6-9s, on paper
levers.risk: Breaks four things at once: every later chunk begins mid-phrase with no context (rules.py:22-26 forbids overlap and has no dedup step; condition_on_previous_text is False), mean_confidence is None so the polish never revisits it (ledger.py:161-164), paragraph breaks vanish because the ledger's gap is always 0 on contiguous chunks (measured) and a 2.5s pause no longer sits inside one chunk for transcriber.py:320 to see, and Whisper's DTW word end times are approximate so the cut clips word onsets. This is the medical-term veto, not a speed tradeoff.

levers.lever: Re-measure the current committed lag before optimising it, using behind_sec already emitted by the socket.
levers.mechanism: web_app.py:1006-1010 computes `behind_sec = time.time() - started - update.audio_sec` per cycle and the developer console reads it via GET /api/debug/events. The +9 to +11s figure in docs/dictation-speed-review.md:13 was recorded 2026-07-28, before the 2026-09-01 tiny.en live-model split that took first words from 15.9s to 4.7s; the committed number may already be lower.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 directly; prevents optimising against a stale baseline
levers.risk: None. Pure measurement.

uncertainties: I did not measure end-to-end committed lag on the running app. The 9-11s target comes from docs/dictation-speed-review.md:13 (recorded 2026-07-28, pre-dating the tiny.en live-model split), so the real current number is unverified and my per-stage seconds are a reconstruction, not an observation.

My decode-cost curve is one clip (data/bench_audio/chest_long.wav), one model (tiny.en), one machine state. Medians run 1.5-2x the minima, so scheduling noise is large and the absolute numbers should not be quoted as budgets; only the shape (cost rises with clip length on tiny.en) is solid.

I did not verify whether Silero's speech_pad_ms=200 merges two marks separated by less than ~400ms. If it does, the effective minimum pause needed to create a cut candidate is nearer 700ms than the 300ms min_silence_duration_ms suggests, and lever 2's payoff changes.

I did not check how often a fully-silent chunk actually occurs in real dictation. My reading is that it needs roughly a 20s force-cut of silence, which would mean the ledger's paragraph break almost never fires today and transcriber.py:320 is doing nearly all the paragraph work. That is inferred from code plus a synthetic ledger run, not from a real recording.
The desktop worker duplicates the commit loop (worker.py:297-339 and :481-506) rather than importing live_session. Every lever above is a two-place change and I only traced the web path in full.

I did not verify that Whisper word end times from tiny.en are accurate enough to cut on. The +0.6 to +1.6s cost of turning them on is measured; their positional error is not, and lever 5 depends entirely on it.

lanes.lane: Is the live loop serialised, and could it overlap work on 16 CPUs?

findings.claim: Audio ingestion is NOT blocked during a decode on the web path any more: the fix on 3ee4324 moved session.cycle() out of the receive loop into an asyncio background task, so ws.receive() keeps draining PCM while a decode runs.
findings.evidence: src/ui/web_app.py:1043-1046 (`if time.time() - last_cycle >= cycle_sec and (cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done()): cycle_task = asyncio.create_task(run_cycle())`) vs the pre-fix `update = await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(session.cycle)` inline in the receive loop; `git show 3ee4324 -- src/ui/web_app.py`. The commit message reports the measured effect: on a 30s clip on-screen lag went from +0.7s->+5.1s (compounding) to +0.05s->+2.7s.

findings.claim: That fix bought drain-freedom, not overlap: the same `cycle_task.done()` guard means exactly one cycle may run at a time, so a chunk that closes while a cycle is in flight is not decoded until that cycle (including its preview decode) has finished.
findings.evidence: src/ui/web_app.py:1043 (the `cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done()` condition) and the comment at src/ui/web_app.py:982-983 ("guards against two decodes running at once, which session.cycle() is not written to survive").

findings.claim: Committed-chunk decode and open-tail preview decode are serialised inside a single Python call: cycle() runs every closed chunk through _commit_closed first, then _decode_open_tail, on one thread.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:205 (`committed_any = self._commit_closed(...)`) then :225 (`preview = self._decode_open_tail(...)`); both call self._decode -> engine.transcribe on the same live_engine (:267-270, :305-308). Desktop mirror: src/dictation/worker.py:306-340 (commit loop) then :359-361 (preview).

findings.claim: Even if the two were run on separate Python threads, ctranslate2 would still serialise them: faster-whisper is constructed without num_workers, so inter_threads=1 and one WhisperModel serves one request at a time.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/transcriber.py:181-183 constructs WhisperModel with only model_ref/device/compute_type/cpu_threads/download_root; faster_whisper 1.2.1 WhisperModel.__init__ defaults num_workers=1 and passes `inter_threads=num_workers` into ctranslate2.models.Whisper (read from installed faster_whisper/transcribe.py).

findings.claim: Measured: two decodes on one shipped-config tiny.en model (cpu_threads=14, num_workers=1) run concurrently take the SAME time as run back-to-back - proof of the CT2 queue, not a thread-pool artefact.
findings.evidence: Benchmark scratchpad/one.py on data/eval/bench/chest_long.wav, 15s + 12s clips, beam=2, 3 reps: `tiny.en intra=14 workers=1: alone15s=2.90 alone12s=2.33 seq=4.64 conc=4.44 speedup=1.05`.

findings.claim: Measured: with num_workers=2 and cpu_threads reduced to 8, the same pair of decodes overlaps for a real win - median for the pair 6.82s (shipped, sequential) -> 4.05s (tuned, concurrent), min 5.20s -> 2.46s, interleaved A/B in one process, 5 reps.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/ab.py: `SHIPPED intra=14 w=1 sequential : min=5.20 med=6.82 max=9.84` / `TUNED intra=8 w=2 concurrent : min=2.46 med=4.05 max=8.31`.

findings.claim: Thread oversubscription is real and measurable: keeping cpu_threads=14 while adding workers gives a much weaker win on tiny.en (28 threads on 16 cores) and an outright LOSS on small.en at beam 5 (42 threads on 16 cores).
findings.evidence: scratchpad/one.py `tiny.en intra=14 workers=2: seq=7.45 conc=3.98 speedup=1.87` vs `tiny.en intra=8 workers=2: seq=3.50 conc=2.31`; scratchpad/polish.py `small.en polish x3(10s,beam5) intra=14 workers=3 par=3: seq=37.80s conc=50.82s speedup=0.74`, against `intra=5 workers=3 par=3: seq=22.46s conc=10.89s speedup=2.06`.

findings.claim: num_workers>1 is not free: ctranslate2 replicates the model per inter-thread, and that measurably degrades even purely sequential throughput - the same 3 sequential small.en decodes cost 13.53s at workers=1 and 37.80s at workers=3.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/polish.py, three separate processes, identical sequential workload: seq=13.53 (intra=14 w=1), seq=37.80 (intra=14 w=3), seq=22.46 (intra=5 w=3). Judged against the shipped baseline the best concurrent polish config is 13.53s -> 10.89s, ~20%, not the 2.06x its own row shows.

findings.claim: The post-Stop confidence-targeted polish decodes chunks strictly one at a time, on both front-ends.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:373-386 (`for done, i in enumerate(targets, ...)` then a blocking self._decode per target, then a further tail decode at :390-394); src/dictation/worker.py:450-476 (same shape, `for done, i in enumerate(targets, ...)` with a blocking engine.transcribe inside).

findings.claim: There is no thread-pool bound capping this: anyio's default thread limiter is 40, and only one to_thread call is ever outstanding per socket anyway.
findings.evidence: anyio._backends._asyncio: `limiter = CapacityLimiter(40)`; the only to_thread calls on the live path are src/ui/web_app.py:995 (cycle), :1072 (close_open_tail_fast) and :1089 (finalize), and the Stop path awaits the in-flight cycle at :1063-1065 before either. The cap is the CT2 inter_threads=1 queue, not the pool.

findings.claim: Because _get_engine caches one AsrEngine per model name process-wide and transcriber._MODEL_CACHE caches the WhisperModel, every socket in the process shares one model object - so with num_workers=1 two browser tabs dictating at once serialise against each other too.
findings.evidence: src/ui/web_app.py:348-360 (`asr_engines` dict under `transcriber_lock`, keyed on the resolved model name); src/dictation/transcriber.py:151-160 + :184 (_MODEL_CACHE keyed on (model_ref, device, compute_type), _MODEL_CACHE_MAX=2 at :90).

findings.claim: Attributing seconds: a closed chunk waits behind the previous cycle's preview decode of the open tail, which alone measured 2.2-2.3s for a 12s tail on tiny.en, on top of its own ~2.5-2.9s decode.
findings.evidence: Component costs measured in scratchpad/one.py (`alone15s=2.90 alone12s=2.33` at the shipped intra=14/w=1 config); the wait is structural per src/ui/web_app.py:1043 and src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:205/225. The docs' own budget puts total felt lag at +9 to +11s with chunk-close policy owning 6-20s of it (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:14-19).

levers.lever: Give the live engine num_workers=2 and drop cpu_threads to ~8, then split cycle() so a closed-chunk commit can start while the previous cycle's preview decode is still running (two guarded tasks in web_app.py's socket loop instead of one `cycle_task`).
levers.mechanism: Today a chunk that closes mid-cycle waits for that cycle's preview decode to finish (live_session.py:205/225, web_app.py:1043), and even a threaded split would queue inside ctranslate2 because inter_threads=1 (transcriber.py:181-183). Both barriers have to go together; then the preview's ~2.3s stops sitting in front of the text that is actually kept.
levers.est_seconds_saved: ~2-3s of committed lag (measured pair cost 6.82s median -> 4.05s median; min 5.20 -> 2.46)
levers.risk: Two risks, both real. (1) Correctness, not accuracy: LiveSession.cycle mutates _ledger, _agreement, _last_stable, _uncertain and _preview_cost with no lock, and web_app.py:982-983 says outright it is not written to survive two callers - the commit path and the preview path must be separated into their own state before this is safe, or the transcript can duplicate or drop a chunk. (2) num_workers=2 replicates the model in RAM and measurably slows sequential decodes (small.en seq 13.53s -> 37.80s at w=3), so cpu_threads must come down in the same change and the pairing must be re-measured, not assumed. Anatomy accuracy is untouched: the same model, beam, prompt and audio bytes go into each transcribe() call, so decoded text should be identical.

levers.lever: Cheaper first step, no concurrency at all: when pending_cuts() shows a chunk is ready to close, skip the preview decode for that cycle outright rather than letting it run after the commit.
levers.mechanism: The preview is cosmetic and never committed (live_session.py:279-287), yet on the very cycle a chunk closes it still costs a full decode that delays the NEXT cycle's commit by ~2.3s. The existing skip machinery (rules.should_skip_preview, _preview_earliest at live_session.py:210-222) already proves dropping a preview is safe and self-healing.
levers.est_seconds_saved: ~1-2s per chunk boundary; no RAM or thread cost
levers.risk: Low. The preview freezes on _last_stable for one cycle, which the code already does under load and shows as STATE_CATCHING_UP. But note docs/dictation-speed-review.md:47 refuted *deleting* the preview entirely because its return value seeds LocalAgreement-2 - this must skip only on chunk-close cycles, where _agreement.reset() is called anyway (live_session.py:206-208), so the seed is being thrown away regardless. That reset is the reason this variant escapes the prior refutation, and it is the thing to verify first.

levers.lever: Run the post-Stop polish chunks concurrently (live_session.py:373-386, worker.py:450-476) with the final engine at num_workers=3, cpu_threads=5.
levers.mechanism: Polish targets are independent chunks by construction (each has its own audio slice and its own ledger index), so nothing orders them; today they queue behind each other for the full beam-5 cost each.
levers.est_seconds_saved: ~2.6s of background time on a 3-chunk polish (measured 13.53s shipped-sequential -> 10.89s), and ZERO on the lag the user is complaining about
levers.risk: Poor value for the risk. It is background time after the report is already handed back (web_app.py:1077-1096), so the radiologist does not sit through it; against that, small.en at intra=14/workers=3 measured a 0.74x LOSS, the ledger.replace() calls would need ordering, and the cancellation check at worker.py:451/479 stops being a clean between-chunks boundary. Do the live-loop levers first and leave this alone.

levers.lever: Do not raise cpu_threads above 14 or add workers without lowering intra threads - and treat any thread-count change as a measured change, not a config tweak.
levers.mechanism: cpu_threads = max(4, os.cpu_count()-2) = 14 here (transcriber.py:167). Two engines each at 14 is already 28 threads on 16 cores whenever the live loop and a polish overlap; adding workers on top is what produced the measured 0.74x regression.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 directly; prevents a 25-35% regression
levers.risk: None to accuracy; this is a guard rail on the levers above rather than a change of its own.

uncertainties: Measurement noise on this machine was large: identical sequential workloads ranged 3.50-9.84s across runs (scratchpad/one.py and ab.py), so every speedup above is quoted as min and median over reps and should be re-confirmed on a quiet machine before anything ships.
The benchmarks call faster_whisper directly, not through the app's AsrEngine port, so they exclude VAD, the postprocess pipeline and the socket - they price decode overlap only, not end-to-end lag.

I did not measure the cross-model case (tiny.en live decode overlapping a small.en polish), which is what actually happens if a second recording starts while a polish is still running; that is the worst oversubscription case and is untested.
Whether splitting cycle() into independently-locked commit and preview halves is achievable without duplicating ledger state is a design question I did not attempt - the 2-3s estimate assumes it is.
num_workers>1 memory cost was not measured, only inferred from the sequential slowdown pattern; on a machine that also holds two Whisper models (transcriber._MODEL_CACHE_MAX=2) that could matter.

The exact validation experiment: start the app, run `python -m scripts.dev.live_probe data/eval/bench/chest_long.wav` five times on shipped code and five times on the patched build, comparing the lag printed on the first update where committed_len grows (not first-text, which is already fixed); then `python -m scripts.eval.run_eval --set tts` on both builds and confirm medical-term error is unchanged - it must be bit-identical, since no decode input changes.

lanes.lane: The decode call itself: what every transcribe() passes, and what faster-whisper 1.2.1 / ctranslate2 4.6.0 offer that this app never touches.

findings.claim: There are exactly three decode shapes. Live committed chunk: beam=live_beam_size(2), vad_filter=False, condition_on_previous_text=False, want_word_confidence=True, temperature=0.0. Open-tail preview: identical but want_word_confidence=False. Post-Stop polish: beam=final_beam_size(5), condition_on_previous_text=True, want_word_confidence=True.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:267-269 (live.chunk), :305-307 (live.preview), :345-347 (stop.tail), :379-381 + :391-393 (final.polish/final.tail), all funnelled through _decode at :414-453; desktop twins at src/dictation/worker.py:320-333 (chunk), :406-417 (preview), :459-470 + :485-496 (polish). Settings src/core/settings.py:43,47.

findings.claim: The temperature fallback ladder is live on two of the six app call sites and is a hidden 8.4x multiplier when it trips. src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:448 pins temperature=0.0 for every web stage, but the desktop polish and the web upload path pass no temperature at all, so TranscribeContext's default None falls through to the 5-value ladder.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/asr/types.py:86 (temperature default None) -> src/dictation/transcriber.py:276 (`temperature if temperature is not None else [0.0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8]`). No temperature passed at src/dictation/worker.py:461-469, :487-495, src/ui/web_app.py:865-871. Measured (bench4, tiny.en, 15s clip, beam=2): temperature=0.0 -> generate()=1, 1.736s; ladder with a threshold forced to always fail -> generate()=5, 13.458s.

findings.claim: A ladder retry is decoder-only, not encoder-only-once-per-temperature: the encoder output is computed once and reused across all 5 passes, but each retry at temperature>0 switches to beam_size=1 with num_hypotheses=best_of (5), so a retry is not cheaper than the greedy pass.
findings.evidence: C:/Python312/Lib/site-packages/faster_whisper/transcribe.py:1432 (`for temperature in options.temperatures`), :1434-1441 (beam_size=1, num_hypotheses=options.best_of), :1445 (generate reuses encoder_output). Measured: encode()=1, generate()=5 for one transcribe() (bench4).

findings.claim: word_timestamps=True does not just add a DTW align pass: on tiny.en it makes the sequential seek loop run a SECOND full 30s-padded encoder+decoder window on the leftover sliver of every clip. Measured encoder windows per transcribe(): 2 with word timestamps, 1 without, at every clip length tested (3/6/7/10/15/20s).
findings.evidence: Cause: transcribe.py:1288-1291 overwrites `seek = round(last_word_end * frames_per_second)` only under `if options.word_timestamps:`; last_word_end lands short of content_frames so the while loop at :1157 runs again. Measured (bench10, tiny.en beam=2): 6s 2.005s/gen=2 vs 0.870s/gen=1; 15s 1.825/gen=2 vs 1.327/gen=1; 20s 2.388/gen=2 vs 1.967/gen=1. align() is called exactly once (bench4).

findings.claim: The docs' claim that dropping word timestamps deletes committed words is VERIFIED in mechanism, but the cited line is stale. With word_timestamps=False a segment's end comes from the coarse timestamp tokens and collapses to the whole clip length; with it on, add_word_timestamps overwrites segment start/end with the first/last word time.
findings.evidence: Overwrite at transcribe.py:1683 (`subsegment['start'] = words[0]['start']`) and :1690 (`subsegment['end'] = words[-1]['end']`); fallback span at transcribe.py:1091-1094 (`end=time_offset + duration`). Measured (bench8, 15s clip): wt=True -> segment (0.0, 14.06); wt=False -> segment (0.0, 15.0). The gate is src/dictation/transcriber.py:385 (`len(lower.split()) <= 2 and duration > 8.0`), NOT transcriber.py:352 as docs/dictation-speed-review.md:51 says - line 352 is the string "amara.org" inside _HALLUCINATION_PHRASES.

findings.claim: faster-whisper 1.2.1 does ship BatchedInferencePipeline, and it helps a SINGLE short clip too, not only a batch, because it bypasses the seek loop entirely: one encode(), one generate(), no second window. Measured on the live model it is 1.27x-2.06x faster than the app's current call at every clip length with word_timestamps=True.
findings.evidence: Class at transcribe.py:111; single generate at :219; one forward per batch at :585-590. Measured (bench10, tiny.en beam=2 wt=True, min of 4): 3s 1.171->0.722 (1.62x); 6s 2.005->0.973 (2.06x); 15s 1.825->1.438 (1.27x); 20s 2.388->1.498 (1.59x). Batched keeps word timestamps (options.word_timestamps honoured at :159-168).

findings.claim: Batching the post-Stop polish chunks into one call is a 2.23x win, because the encoder runs one batched forward pass instead of four.
findings.evidence: Measured (bench7, tiny.en beam=2 wt=True, 4 chunks of 7s = the shape of _run_confidence_targeted_polish at src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:376-397): sequential 4x transcribe() 6.830s vs BatchedInferencePipeline 3.060s.

findings.claim: BatchedInferencePipeline silently overrides three things the app's polish path sets on purpose: condition_on_previous_text is forced False, the temperature list is truncated to its first value, and hallucination_silence_threshold is forced None. max_initial_timestamp also changes from 1.0 to 0.0.
findings.evidence: transcribe.py:547 (condition_on_previous_text=False), :528-532 (temperature[:1]), :546 (hallucination_silence_threshold=None), :552 (max_initial_timestamp=0.0). The polish sites pass condition_on_previous_text=True: src/dictation/worker.py:466, :492 and src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:381, :393.

findings.claim: Batched output is NOT byte-identical to the current call: 6 of 10 eval clips differed. The medical-term direction leaned in favour of batched (pleural vs plural, lymphadenopathy vs lymphoidinopathy, ascites vs sides) but it lost one (Mediastinal -> Mediastinol). This is a lead, not a result: it has not been through scripts/eval.
findings.evidence: Measured (bench11, tiny.en beam=2 wt=True, data/eval/tts/report_000..009.wav): identical text 4/10; diffs printed above; sequential total 28.5s vs batched 23.1s (1.23x).

findings.claim: There is NO supported way to decode a window shorter than 30 seconds. chunk_length only resizes the feature extractor's stride; every window is still padded back to 3000 mel frames before the encoder, so setting it smaller just buys MORE full-cost windows.
findings.evidence: Hard-coded pad at faster_whisper/audio.py:111 (`def pad_or_trim(array, length: int = 3000)`), applied unconditionally at transcribe.py:1180 (sequential) and :515 (batched); chunk_length only mutates n_samples/nb_max_frames at feature_extractor.py:203-205. Measured (bench3, 15s clip): chunk_length=None min 1.734s, chunk_length=10 min 2.704s - slower, as the source predicts.

findings.claim: cpu_threads = max(4, cpu_count-2) = 14 is past the optimum on this 16-CPU machine. An interleaved sweep on the live model put the minimum at 6-8 threads, about 13% faster than 14.
findings.evidence: Setting at src/dictation/transcriber.py:167. Measured (bench6, tiny.en, 15s clip, beam=2, wt=True, 6 interleaved reps, min): 2 threads 1.734s, 4 1.268, 6 1.089, 8 1.062, 10 1.152, 14 1.233. Caveat: the machine carried ~60% background load throughout, so absolute numbers are inflated; the ranking is from interleaved reps so it is load-fair.

findings.claim: num_workers is never passed, so ctranslate2 runs with inter_threads=1. Two decodes from two Python threads still overlap under inter_threads=1 (they are not serialised), but oversubscribing 2x14 threads on 16 CPUs costs about a quarter of the theoretical gain; num_workers=2 with cpu_threads=7 recovers nearly all of it.
findings.evidence: src/dictation/transcriber.py:180-183 passes only cpu_threads/download_root; faster_whisper/transcribe.py:694-695 maps cpu_threads->intra_threads, num_workers->inter_threads. Measured (bench5, tiny.en 15s clip, speedup vs 2x solo): 14/1 = 1.47x; 14/2 = 1.78x; 7/2 = 1.95x (and solo dropped from 2.228s to 1.764s).

findings.claim: The app never runs two decodes concurrently today, so num_workers only becomes a lever if the preview decode is deliberately overlapped with the committed-chunk decode. The web live loop explicitly refuses to start a cycle while one is in flight, and the desktop runs one QThread.
findings.evidence: src/ui/web_app.py:1043 (`if time.time() - last_cycle >= cycle_sec and (cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done())`); both decodes happen inside one session.cycle() at src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:267 then :305, sequentially.

findings.claim: Options faster-whisper 1.2.1 exposes that appear nowhere in the app: without_timestamps, best_of, patience, max_new_tokens, hallucination_silence_threshold, prefix, no_repeat_ngram_size, repetition_penalty, length_penalty, clip_timestamps, batch_size, num_workers, chunk_length. Of these, without_timestamps was measured and is NOT a win on its own.
findings.evidence: grep over src/ and scripts/ for all of these names returns no ASR hits (only unrelated tempfile prefix= uses). Sequential default is without_timestamps=False (transcribe.py:776) vs batched True (:283). Measured (bench8, 15s, interleaved x5): False min 1.740s vs True min 1.727s - inside noise, and it makes the segment span the whole clip, which arms the 8-second gate.

levers.lever: Route the live committed-chunk decode through BatchedInferencePipeline with clip_timestamps=[{start:0, end:clip_len}] and batch_size=1, keeping word_timestamps=True. The app already hands transcribe() exactly one pre-cut VAD chunk, which is precisely the input clip_timestamps wants, so nothing about chunking changes.
levers.mechanism: The sequential path runs the seek loop twice per clip on tiny.en because transcribe.py:1291 re-seeks to last_word_end, which lands inside the clip. Batched has no seek loop: one encode(), one generate(). Measured generate() drops 2 -> 1.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0.5-0.9s per committed chunk on tiny.en (20s chunk: 2.388s -> 1.498s measured); roughly 1-1.5s of the 9-11s felt lag, since one committed chunk sits on the critical path at a time
levers.risk: Highest-risk item on the list for the veto metric: text is not identical (6/10 eval clips differed). The medical terms leaned better (pleural, lymphadenopathy, ascites all came out RIGHT in batched and WRONG in sequential) but Mediastinal regressed. Must go through scripts/eval before it ships. Batched also silently forces condition_on_previous_text=False (transcribe.py:547) - harmless here, the live chunk already passes False.

levers.lever: Batch the post-Stop confidence-targeted polish: collect the low-confidence chunk indices and send them as one BatchedInferencePipeline call with their clip_timestamps, instead of the per-chunk loop.
levers.mechanism: One batched encoder forward for N chunks instead of N encoder passes, each of which currently pads to a 30s window regardless of the chunk being 6-20s.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 2.23x on the polish pass (measured 6.830s -> 3.060s for 4x7s chunks on tiny.en); does not touch the 9-11s live lag, it shortens the post-Stop wait
levers.risk: Batched forces condition_on_previous_text=False, and the polish sites deliberately pass True (worker.py:466, live_session.py:381) so each re-decoded chunk currently inherits the prior chunk's tokens. Losing that could cost cross-chunk continuity, which is exactly where anatomy terms carry over. Also drops the temperature ladder (see next lever, which makes that a benefit). Progress reporting per chunk would need reworking.

levers.lever: Pin temperature=0.0 on the two call sites that currently leave it None: src/dictation/worker.py:461-469 and :487-495 (desktop post-Stop polish) and src/ui/web_app.py:865-871 (upload path). The web live path already does this at live_session.py:448.
levers.mechanism: TranscribeContext's None default falls through to transcriber.py:276's 5-temperature ladder. When compression_ratio or log_prob trips, one transcribe() makes five generate() calls; measured 1.736s -> 13.458s on tiny.en, and the polish runs at beam=5 on small.en where each pass is far dearer. It is a tail-latency landmine, and it is inconsistent between the two front-ends, which is a known failure mode in this repo.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 in the median case, up to ~8x the polish decode in the tail. Removes a multi-second unpredictable stall after Stop
levers.risk: Real, and it points the other way on accuracy: the ladder exists to rescue a chunk whose greedy decode collapsed into repetition. Deleting it means such a chunk keeps its garbage. The safer form is a 2-value ladder [0.0, 0.2] rather than 5, or leaving it and simply making both front-ends agree. Needs scripts/eval before choosing.

levers.lever: Drop cpu_threads from max(4, cpu_count-2)=14 to a configured value around 6-8 in src/dictation/transcriber.py:167, and put it in dictation_settings.json rather than deriving it in source.
levers.mechanism: CTranslate2 intra-op threading on the small encoder/decoder matmuls of tiny.en saturates well before 14 threads; past the knee the synchronisation cost dominates. Measured minimum at 6-8 threads.
levers.est_seconds_saved: ~0.17s per decode on tiny.en (1.233s -> 1.062s), so ~13%. Small but free and zero accuracy risk
levers.risk: None for accuracy - thread count cannot change the arithmetic result of a beam search in CTranslate2. The measurement was taken on a machine at ~60% background load; the optimum may sit higher on an idle machine, which is exactly why this belongs in config rather than a hard-coded formula.

levers.lever: Overlap the open-tail preview decode with the committed-chunk decode: pass num_workers=2 to WhisperModel (transcriber.py:180-183), drop cpu_threads to ~7, and run the two decodes of one cycle on two threads instead of back to back at live_session.py:267 then :305.
levers.mechanism: Today one cycle pays chunk-decode time PLUS preview-decode time serially. Measured, two concurrent 15s decodes at cpu_threads=7/num_workers=2 finish in 1.95x the throughput of running them one after the other, and solo latency also improved (2.228s -> 1.764s).
levers.est_seconds_saved: roughly the preview decode's own cost per cycle, ~1-1.5s of the cycle time, which is what currently delays the next committed chunk
levers.risk: Memory: inter_threads=2 loads a second model replica. Ordering: the preview and the commit both mutate session state (_agreement, _ledger) and would need the commit to win. The 'no un-writing' invariant depends on the preview seeing the ledger AFTER the commit, so a naive parallelisation could show a word twice or take one back. Needs care, not a one-line change.

levers.lever: Drop want_word_confidence from the committed-chunk decode AFTER first fixing the 8-second gate at src/dictation/transcriber.py:385 to skip rule 2 when the segment has no words.
levers.mechanism: Measured, word timestamps cost a whole extra 30s-padded encoder+decoder window on tiny.en (generate() 2 -> 1), not the small DTW pass the docs assumed. That is 0.42s on a 20s chunk and 1.13s on a 6s chunk.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0.4-1.1s per committed chunk
levers.risk: Refuted as written, and the refutation is real: without word timestamps a segment's end becomes the whole clip length (measured 15.0 vs 14.06), so any chunk decoding to <=2 words is silently deleted by transcriber.py:385. It also kills polish_confidence_ceiling targeting and the faint low-confidence underline, both of which are anatomy-safety surfaces. Only worth it if the batched lever above turns out not to be viable, since batched gets the same single-window benefit WITHOUT giving up confidence.

levers.lever: Set without_timestamps=True on the decode kwargs at src/dictation/transcriber.py:255-278.
levers.mechanism: Fewer tokens for the decoder to emit autoregressively.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 - measured 1.740s vs 1.727s on a 15s clip, inside noise, because the app's chunks produce a single segment and therefore only two timestamp tokens
levers.risk: It collapses segment end to the full clip length, which arms the same 8-second hallucination gate. No upside measured, real downside. Do not do this.

levers.lever: Shorten the 30-second encoder window via chunk_length.
levers.mechanism: Would cut encoder work proportionally if the window were resizable.
levers.est_seconds_saved: 0 - it is not supported. pad_or_trim's length=3000 is a hard-coded default (audio.py:111) applied at transcribe.py:1180 and :515
levers.risk: Measured net slower: chunk_length=10 on a 15s clip cost 2.704s vs 1.734s, because it splits one full-cost window into two full-cost windows. It also mutates the shared FeatureExtractor's n_samples in place (feature_extractor.py:203-205), which would leak across the process-wide model cache at transcriber.py:84.

uncertainties: Every absolute timing here was taken on a machine running at roughly 60% background CPU load (a 'herdr' process, Chrome, several Claude sessions). Interleaved min-of-N was used throughout to make comparisons load-fair, but absolute seconds are inflated and medians swung 2-10x. Re-measure on an idle machine before quoting any number to the user.

The double-encoder-window effect from word_timestamps was measured on tiny.en (the live model, the one on the critical path) at every clip length. On small.en at beam=5 it did NOT appear (generate()=1 both ways) and the batched win shrank to 0.96-1.18x. The size of the batched win is therefore model- and content-dependent, and I only proved it for the model that actually decodes the committed chunks.

The 6-out-of-10 text differences between sequential and batched are a lead, not a measurement of accuracy. Nothing here went through scripts/eval, so no WER or medical-term-error number backs the claim that batched is accuracy-neutral or better. That harness run is the gate on the top two levers.

I did not test whether BatchedInferencePipeline is thread-safe or whether one pipeline instance can be shared across the live loop and the polish pass; the class holds mutable state (self.last_speech_timestamp, transcribe.py:117).

The estimated end-to-end seconds saved assume the committed-chunk decode sits directly on the critical path between speech and permanent text. The docs (docs/dictation-speed-review.md) say 6-20s of the 9-11s lag is chunk-close policy, not decode, so a decode win of 1s may show up as less than 1s of felt improvement.
I did not verify whether ctranslate2 4.6.0's int8 kernels behave differently from float32 with respect to the cpu_threads knee; only int8 (the app's resolved compute type) was measured.

On small.en (the post-Stop accuracy model, settings final_beam_size=5) beam 5 costs 33% more wall and 22% more CPU than beam 2, and beam 2 costs 20% more than beam 1, on a 10s clip.

findings.claim: The app's cpu_threads setting is past the knee: 14 threads is SLOWER than 8 on this machine. A 10s tiny.en decode takes 1.007s at 8 threads vs 1.405s at 14 (28% faster) and uses 21% less CPU.
findings.evidence: b3.py threads, tiny.en 10s, best-of-5 interleaved. wall_min / cpu_min by cpu_threads: 2 -> 2.066/4.44; 4 -> 1.488/4.80; 6 -> 1.093/6.05; 8 -> 1.007/6.73; 10 -> 1.017/7.89; 14 -> 1.405/8.47; 16 -> 1.223/8.89. Overlapping only pays once you give it a second worker or a second model instance: two 10s decodes finish in 1.526s on two 7-thread models vs 2.132s sequential (28% faster), or 1.775s with num_workers=2 (17% faster).

The app never sets num_workers, so it is 1: src/dictation/transcriber.py:180-183 passes only model_ref, device, compute_type, cpu_threads, download_root.

findings.claim: faster_whisper.BatchedInferencePipeline exists in 1.2.1 and is 27-36% faster in wall and 21-35% cheaper in CPU on tiny.en, but it takes ONE audio input, so batching four separate chunks is not a native operation, and part of the win is its forced internal VAD trimming silence rather than faster compute.
findings.evidence: b3.py batched, tiny.en, best-of-4 wall_min / cpu_min: plain 10s 1.951/10.50; batched 10s bs=1 1.285/6.97; batched 10s bs=4 1.240/6.83; plain 25s 2.592/12.66; batched 25s bs=4 2.589/10.03; plain 30.5s 3.033/14.83; batched 30.5s bs=8 2.554/11.70. bs=1 and bs=4 being identical on a continuous clip shows the batch axis is VAD segments inside one clip, not clips. The mechanism is real but the 3-second figure is wrong by roughly 2-3x and is a worst case that cannot be reached.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (read in code):
- Ordering is as stated: `_commit_closed(...)` at src/dictation/stream/live_session.py:205, `_decode_open_tail(...)` at live_session.py:225, both inside the single-threaded `cycle()` (live_session.py:185).
- Serialisation is real: the cycle runs on one worker thread (`anyio.to_thread.run_sync(session.cycle)`, src/ui/web_app.py:995) and a new cycle is refused while one is in flight (`cycle_task is None or cycle_task.done()`, web_app.py:1043). So a chunk that becomes closable mid-cycle cannot be committed until the in-flight preview decode returns.

WHY THE NUMBER FAILS:
1. The wait is bounded by exactly ONE preview call, not three seconds. I measured the model the app actually runs (`live_model_size: "tiny.en"`, src/core/settings.py:86 and dictation_settings.json:54) at beam 2 on data/eval/bench/chest_long.wav: best-of-three 0.76s / 1.03s / 1.38s / 1.76s / 1.55s for 3/6/10/15/20s clips (worst single call 2.55s). Matches the existing measured table in docs/dictation-speed-review.md:130-138. One preview cannot cost 3s.
2. Previews only occupy about half the cycles anyway: `self._preview_earliest = time.time() + cost` (live_session.py:313) blocks the next preview for as long as the last one took (checked at live_session.py:212). So a closing chunk is delayed only ~50% of the time, and the expected wait is a fraction of one decode (~0.4-0.7s), not the worst case.
3. There is already a MEASURED ceiling that contradicts 3s: deleting the open-tail preview decode entirely moved end-to-end lag from +10.5s to +9.1s, i.e. 1.4s total, "about 13% of the lag" (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:34-37) — and that was measured when the live path used a slower model. Removing the preview removes both its own cycle occupancy AND the serialisation the claim describes, so 1.4s is the hard upper bound on everything the claim covers.
4. The "3 seconds" looks like it was read off `preview_max_lag_sec: 3.0` (src/core/settings.py:53, dictation_settings.json:47). That constant is the threshold above which a preview is SKIPPED (`should_skip_preview`, src/dictation/stream/rules.py), not a delay anyone waits. With measured preview cost ~0.8-1.8s it never fires, so that path contributes 0s.
5. The claim also mis-locates the worse half of the same effect. Within one cycle the committed text is not sent until AFTER the preview: `_commit_closed` (205) → preview (225) → LiveUpdate built (231) → returned → `send()` (web_app.py:1017). So a freshly committed chunk waits behind the preview in its OWN cycle, not merely behind the previous one's. Same bound: one decode call.

WHAT ACTUALLY OWNS THE 9-11s: chunk-close latency by construction — `chunk_min_sec` 6.0 / `chunk_soft_max_sec` 15.0 / `chunk_force_cut_sec` 20.0 (dictation_settings.json:40-42, src/dictation/stream/segmenter.py:31-33). Nothing is committed until a VAD pause at or after 6s, so 6-15s of the lag is policy, not queueing (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:19 records this as "6-20 s by construction").
verdicts.correction: Preview/commit serialisation is real but worth well under 1.5 seconds, not 3. Because `cycle()` is single-threaded and the socket refuses a new cycle while one is in flight (live_session.py:185/205/225, web_app.py:995,1043), a closing chunk can queue behind at most ONE open-tail preview decode — measured at 0.76-1.76s best-of-three on the live model the app runs (tiny.en, beam 2), worst single call 2.55s. The `_preview_earliest` throttle (live_session.py:313) means previews run in only about half of cycles, so the expected penalty is ~0.4-0.7s. The measured ceiling for the whole effect is 1.4s: deleting the preview decode outright moved lag 10.5s→9.1s (docs/dictation-speed-review.md:34-37). The "3 seconds" is `preview_max_lag_sec` (settings.py:53), a skip threshold that never fires at current decode costs, not a wait. The dominant term in the 9-11s committed lag remains chunk-close policy: `chunk_min_sec` 6.0 / `chunk_soft_max_sec` 15.0.

verdicts.correction: After a cut exists, the web loop's scheduling delay before the cut is picked up is max(live_cycle_sec, time left in the in-flight cycle), not their sum: `last_cycle` is stamped at task creation (web_app.py:1044), so the 0.5 s window overlaps the running cycle. Measured: (a) the effective silence requirement is 352ms, not 300ms, because Silero tests silence in 512-sample (32ms) windows with a strict `<` (faster_whisper/vad.py:131-137); (b) the 200ms pad is halved to exactly half the gap for pauses under 400ms (faster_whisper/vad.py:157-168), which makes the padded marks touch and makes segmenter.py:94-98's strict `end < next_start` reject them, so the true floor for a usable pause is 416ms - pauses of 352-384ms produce marks but no chunk cut at all; (c) the 200ms pad adds zero wall-clock delay for pauses >= 416ms, it only extends the closed chunk 200ms into the silence (measured cut at 7.176s for speech ending at 6.976s); (d) the dominant delay the claim omits is that a chunk cannot close until the speaker STARTS TALKING AGAIN - with only one speech mark there is no `marks[i+1]`, so 7s of speech followed by 1000ms of continuing silence yields zero closed chunks, and the wait is the whole pause plus ~32ms, unbounded until force_cut_sec=20s. Net: the pause gate costs roughly (pause duration + 32ms), with a hard 416ms floor, not 0.5s - and it is dwarfed by ChunkPolicy min_sec=6.0 / soft_max_sec=15.0, which is the real structural source of the 9-11s committed lag.
